items.title: 17.4 Thermal Decomposition of Carbonates and Nitrates

source_refs.note: Topic 17.4 with Table 17.3 and Quick Check 17.2, answered (PDF 8-10); the book's polarisation sketch is replaced by an original diagram. Answers were derived and need review.

blocks.text: Thermal decomposition is a reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances when heated; it usually needs energy (it is endothermic) to break bonds. It is useful for studying Group 2 carbonates and nitrates because their thermal stability follows a clear trend.

items: Carbonates decompose to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide, e.g. MgCO3(s) -> MgO(s) + CO2(g) and CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g). Their stability increases down the group: BeCO3 decomposes at the lowest temperature and BaCO3 needs the highest.

Nitrates decompose to the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, e.g. 2Ca(NO3)2(s) -> 2CaO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g). Their stability also increases down the group: Be(NO3)2 is the least stable and Ba(NO3)2 the most stable.

blocks.alt: Two panels. Left: a small Mg2+ ion beside a carbonate ion whose dashed electron cloud is pulled out of shape towards the ion. Right: a large Ba2+ ion beside a carbonate ion whose cloud is nearly round. A note gives decomposition temperatures of 540 C for MgCO3 and 1360 C for BaCO3.
blocks.caption: Polarisation of the carbonate ion by small and large cations (original diagram for the book's sketch).
blocks.long_description: A small, doubly charged cation such as Mg2+ has a high charge density, so it pulls on the electron cloud of the large carbonate ion and distorts (polarises) it. This weakens bonds within the carbonate ion, which then breaks into CO2 and an oxide ion at a lower temperature. Down the group the cations are larger, polarise the anion less, and the carbonates become more stable: MgCO3 decomposes at 540 C but BaCO3 needs 1360 C. Nitrates follow the same trend.

blocks.text: The trend is explained by polarising power. Small, highly charged cations such as Be2+ distort the large carbonate (or nitrate) ion more, weakening its bonds so that it decomposes more easily. Larger cations lower in the group polarise the anion less, so their carbonates and nitrates need more heat.

blocks.caption: Decomposition temperatures of Group 2 carbonates at 1 atm (book's Table 17.3)

blocks.text: By observing the temperature at which a Group 2 carbonate or nitrate decomposes, chemists can help identify unknown compounds; the pattern shows the link between ionic size, charge density and thermal stability.

items: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of SrCO3, and explain why MgCO3 is less stable than CaCO3.
Write equations for the decomposition of magnesium nitrate and barium nitrate. Which decomposes at a lower temperature?
